title: The Platonic Solids: Inside the five, the five filling space, and where the five live
description:
The Platonic Solids: Inside the five, the five filling space, and where the five live is Book Eight (Wind) of The Five Orders of Space, by DICTO. It follows the five regular solids, the dodecahedron, icosahedron, cube, tetrahedron and octahedron (D·I·C·T·O), inside one another, filling space, and in four dimensions, asking where all five are at home together, the icosahedron included, in an Opening, fourteen chapters in three parts, an Epilogue and a Coda.

Opening, The Outsider: the icosahedron fills no space alone, even in four-dimensional curved space; the book's question, and a second outsider, the DICTO Ogdoecontahedron (OG, #31). Part One, Inside the five. Chapter 1, The Nest: Euclid's cube in the dodecahedron, Pacioli's icosahedron in the octahedron and Kepler's nest close into one periodic cell holding all five, and twelve classical inscriptions give fourteen chains through all five (#8, #99). Chapter 2, Two Golden Cuts Each: every Platonic solid has exactly two golden cuts, ten in all; on the octahedron they are Icosaxes and Unborn Axes, which fill space together, and no point set over ℚ(√5) holds a Golden Cut Cube (#88, #90). Chapter 3, Aristotle's Pyramids: a set of the five face pyramids fills space exactly when it is the cube's alone, the tetrahedron's with the octahedron's, or both; face to face, the tetrahedron's and octahedron's pyramids tile exactly as the close-packed stackings (#44, #77, #92). Chapter 4, The Vacuus: the walls between a solid's centre pyramids, their angles read from the polar solid and their central discs from the symmetry: the octahedron has three square discs, the other four none (#87, #107). Chapter 5, The Round Five: balls on the corners of each solid make five round bodies of smallest width exactly 1 (#45).

Part Two, The five fill space. Chapter 6, The Chain of Karma: the dodecahedron is an icosahedron in a shell of 12 pentagonal pyramids, 30 AXE and 20 CLEO, and the shells alternate without end (#19, #22). Chapter 7, The Dogstar: dodecahedra on alternate cubes leave Hart's Dogstar, of volume exactly φ/2, and the two fill space (#42). Chapter 8, Every Mix Fills Space: every one of the 31 mixes of the five fills space with a kit of seven connectors (#47). Chapter 9, One World: each of the five fits in a skin that makes it a dodecahedron, so every mix lives on one cubic grid (#106). Chapter 10, Filigree: the connectors read as gold round stones, each a setting, ground or edging; at edge 1 the icosahedron's setting fills exactly a dodecahedron's place, so the two share one golden slab with no edging, three mixes need no gold at all, and jewellery figures (ring, bracelet, brooch, pendant, necklace, earrings) show the pieces at work. Chapter 11, Plato's Five in the Octet: every cell of the octet holds all five, nested, for ever by thirds (#99, #8, #41).

Part Three, Where the five live. Chapter 12, The Residents: in four dimensions four of the five fill curved space alone, the icosahedron only with the tetrahedron, and of the polytopes of the four four-dimensional reflection groups only the family of the 600-cell and the 120-cell houses all five among its corners, proved with every resident counted exactly (#108). Chapter 13, Beyond the Five: three families of the five go on in every dimension; the golden line of the dodecahedron and the icosahedron stops in the fourth, and with Schläfli's count the classical subject closes. Chapter 14, Towards the Quasicrystal: a ladder of crystals climbs from the octet to five-fold order, a nest on every icosahedral seat; on the hidden side of the OG (its Galois twin, √5 → −√5) the regular icosahedron and dodecahedron appear exactly.

Epilogue, What has been shown: the conclusion, every main claim with its status, and open problems. Coda, The Elements: Plato's elements and DICTO's colours. Appendix: sources by chapter; papers in this book and papers referred to; references; index; the series page of The Five Orders of Space.

125 pages. Cover by DICTO: the five Platonic solids at equal volume, see-through, on a circle in D·I·C·T·O order, the dodecahedron at the top. Computation, verification and drafting with Claude (Anthropic). Licence CC BY-SA 4.0. More at dictospheres.com.
